did_you_know.text: Did you know? The Passover described here was the only one the Israelites celebrated in the desert for forty years, besides the very first one.

Did you know? The institution of "Pesach Sheni" (Second Passover), an additional Passover in the second month, was not commanded in advance, but came as a direct response to the question and request of impure individuals who wished to observe the commandment.

Did you know? "Pesach Sheni" (Second Passover) illustrates the desire that no one be left out: it allowed people who were ritually impure or far away to fulfill the commandment of the sacrifice, even a month later.
Did you know? The commandment of "Pesach Sheni" emphasizes that the laws of the Torah apply equally to everyone: "one statute shall be for you and for the stranger and for the native of the land."

Did you know? The pillar of cloud by day and fire by night that covered the Tabernacle were not just natural phenomena, but a constant and tangible manifestation of God's direct presence and guidance during the Israelites' journey in the desert.

Did you know? All the movements of the Israelites, when to travel and when to camp, were dictated exclusively by the cloud, emphasizing their complete dependence and obedience to God's will without human consideration.

Did you know? The duration of the Israelites' stops in the desert was unpredictable – from one night to many days, a month, or more – which taught them patience and trust in God, and required them to be in constant readiness.

Did you know? The phrase "they kept the charge of the Lord" emphasizes that the Israelites not only traveled and camped according to God's will, but also maintained full commitment to divine guidance in all aspects of their lives.
